doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

title: Studio musicians, Steve Gadd and staying on one chord
summary: Studio players in New York asked about changes; Wesley and Monk Rowe discuss avoiding boredom on a one-chord groove.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: have the music written out. I remember Steve Gadd would play stuff that if you never thought to write, but he would just play things you know with the bass player. What was his name? I can’t think of his name right now. But he’d ask me, say, “Well where are the changes?” I’d say, “There are no changes here.”

[Scats]. And he refused to do that. But when I finally broke him down to where he would do it, he did the hell out of it. So some things happened automatically, some things happened just because they were written down and they played it exactly like it was written you know.

I was thinking, while you were just saying that, I thought of Pharoah Sanders because a lot of his music stayed on one chord for a long time. And I don’t have a question here except that it seems like you have to have a long attention span and just get into that rhythm so much that it doesn’t become boring. Because if it becomes boring it’s not going to work.
Right. Well I can’t think of this bass player’s name.

No. Anyway you are exactly right, if it becomes boring to them then it’s not happening you know. But if it fits with the other music and the other musicians, and they lock it in together and it becomes good to you, you know, what you play becomes really good to your soul you know, you love to do it. And when you do it, you do it automatically, without even thinking about it, and the same notes or the same chords become wonderful chords to you and you don’t get bored.
